title: Cell-Soothe: developing a self-harm app for women in prison
official: Cell-Soothe: the feasibility and acceptability of a digital app for women who self-harm in prison
summary:
Background and study aims
Self-harm is an ongoing problem in women's prisons, where the number and rate of incidents is the highest it has been since 2004. Although the self-harm rate is high, there is little reliable information on how to prevent self-harm, or to support women who self-harm. Mobile applications (apps) are well-suited to prisons, as these can be used in women's cells when they are alone and more likely to self-harm. They can also be adapted based on women's literacy levels and other needs. This project aims to work with staff and women in prisons to design a new app for women prisoners who self-harm. This app will be a programme that can be downloaded and used on in-cell laptops. It will help women with their thoughts about self-harm, so that they are less likely to hurt themselves. We will also speak to experts to work out how the app could be provided to people in prisons, and how we could test whether it reduces self-harm, once we develop it.

Who can participate?
In the first part of the study, we want to interview digital prison decision makers about the challenges of creating and using digital interventions in prisons. Next, we will interview prison and healthcare staff at two women’s prisons in England and Wales to discuss what should and shouldn’t be included in a self-harm app. We will also interview women in prison who have self-harmed in the last six months to see what content they would prefer. Then, in the final part of the study, we want to conduct workshops with experts to assess the best way to test if the app effectively reduces self-harm.

What does the study involve?
The study will involve completing a consent form, and then attending an interview or a workshop with a member of the research team. The interviews and workshops will take place either face-to-face or online on MS Teams. The interviews will last around an hour, whilst the workshops will take up to 90 minutes. The interviews and workshops will be audio or video recorded, if people agree to this.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
There are no direct benefits to people who participate. However, their involvement will help us to learn more about digital self-harm interventions, including how these might be used to better prevent self-harm, or support women who self-harm, in prison. Because the study focuses on self-harm, there is a risk that people might experience some discomfort or distress while talking about this topic.

Where is the study run from?
This study is being conducted by GMMH NHS Foundation Trust, and is being led by Dr. Kerry Gutridge and Dr. Louise Robinson at the University of Manchester.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
The interviews and workshops will start in October 2026 and finish in November 2027.

Who is funding the study?
The study is being funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR).

Who is the main contact?
Dr Kerry Gutridge, kerry.gutridge@manchester.ac.uk

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Professionals:
1. Aged 18 or over
2. Have the relevant expertise or professional role for the research phase

Women who self-harm in prison:
1. 18 years or over
2. Remand and sentenced prisoners with personal experience of self-harm in prison in the last six months
Exclusion criteria:
Professionals:
1. Aged under 18
2. Do not have the relevant expertise or professional role for the research phase
3. Do not consent to being recorded (workshops only)

Women who self-harm in prison:
1. Aged under 18 years
2. Unable to provide informed consent
3. Unable to take part in an interview in English
4. Women where risk to others means that individual interviews could not be conducted
5. Women who are too distressed/unwell to participate
